answers.why: Ephraim makes treaties with Assyria and sends oil to Egypt.
The LORD's controversy with Judah accompanies judgment on the people described as making foreign treaties.
Ephraim boasts of wealth amid accusations of dishonest trade and oppression.
Israel is Jacob, who fled to Aram and tended sheep to obtain a wife.
The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt through a prophet.
Ephraim's provocation and bloodguilt continue the indictment of the people delivered from Egypt.
Ephraim incurred guilt through Baal worship, and the next verse describes their continuing idolatry.
Israel is the nation within which Ephraim held an exalted position.
Israel is addressed as having cities, judges, and a demand for a king.
Ephraim's stored guilt belongs to the people whose king God gave and removed.
The call for Israel to return continues with plural commands to repent and speak to the LORD.
Israel's flourishing follows God's promise to heal their backsliding and love them.
Ephraim's rejection of idols concludes the promise of the people's restoration.
